endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Additionally, HDOs should define explicit conditions under which an AI solution will not proceed to deployment, including: Unmitigated high-severity harm potential that cannot be reduced through available controls;

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: The team should also determine whether safety concerns meeting the defined risk threshold at one health system (thereby triggering a delay in the pilot phase and re-evaluation) are shared with the developer organization and regulator(s), as appropriate.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether prohibiting deployment above a residual-risk tolerance, or limiting post-failure deployment to bounded pilots with halt criteria, reduces harm from AI in health care. The recommendation rests on two CHAI framework documents that use "should" language, and no study documenting the hazard was supplied either.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no body of evidence exists to rate for design, consistency, directness, or precision. Under GRADE conventions the certainty is no direct evidence. The two endorsements are expert consensus statements, and consensus does not substitute for outcome data.

Both endorsing sources are voluntary CHAI frameworks rather than statutes or agency rules. One asks health systems to define explicit no-go conditions for unmitigated high-severity harm. The other asks whether safety concerns that trigger a pilot delay should be shared with developers and regulators. Neither source sets a numeric tolerance or specifies halt criteria.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without predefined residual-risk tolerances and pilot halt criteria. Such studies would measure how often deployments are stopped or delayed, whether halted tools would have caused harm, and how often bounded pilots reach their halt criteria. Descriptive work documenting how often AI is deployed with unmitigated high-severity risk would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from the supplied evidence whether risk tolerances set by governance bodies account for harms that fall disproportionately on these groups.
